syllabus.clause: the same deferral mechanism underlies Airflow 3.1 human-in-the-loop operators and deadline alerts

items.item: standard operators and sensors occupy a full worker slot for their entire runtime, even while idle
deferring hands execution to the triggerer, which frees the worker for the deferred phase of execution
triggers should avoid persistent state so they can be serialized and moved around freely between triggerer hosts

at.step: Reveal: trigger serialization, corrupted not crashed

items.item: a triggerer defaults to a capacity of a thousand triggers at once; past that, some are delayed until others complete
poke mode takes up a worker slot for a sensor's entire runtime; reschedule only while actively checking
Airflow 3.1 introduced Human-in-the-Loop functionality, pausing tasks in a deferred state to wait for human input
a later changelog entry confirms the awaiting_input task state for Human-in-the-Loop runs off the triggerer
Airflow 3.1 also introduced Deadline Alerts, firing a callback when a DAG run exceeds a time threshold

The worker-occupancy measurement in this topic isolates a variable most worker-slot-hours arguments leave implicit: the same operator, same wait, same cap, run twice. That controls out every confound (different sensors have different overhead) and leaves only the one real difference — whether the wait itself happens inside a worker process or outside one.

A reader who assumes deferral is strictly better than poke mode is missing the real trade this topic measured: the deferred run took over three times longer in wall-clock time for the identical wait, because handing a task back to the scheduler and routing it through the triggerer costs real round-trip latency that polling in place does not.

items.item: The trigger serialization finding here is stronger than 'serialization can fail' — Airflow's BaseSerialization doesn't fail at all on an unserializable kwarg; it falls back to a string representation. That means a broken trigger passes every check available at defer time and only reveals itself later, which is a materially worse failure mode for an author to debug than an upfront crash.

at.step: Reveal: trigger serialization, corrupted not crashed

items.item: Deferring and mode='reschedule' are frequently conflated because both 'release the worker between checks,' but reschedule still occupies a worker during every check and re-polls on a fixed timer, while deferring hands the entire wait to a different process and resumes only when the trigger itself observes the condition — there is no polling interval for the task to re-enter on.

The triggerer's default capacity of a thousand per process, and max_trigger_to_select_per_loop defaulting to fifty, are two different knobs solving two different problems: capacity bounds how much one triggerer host will attempt; the per-loop limit exists specifically to keep multiple HA triggerer hosts from starving each other when load is unevenly distributed.

By default, a deferred task does not occupy a pool slot either, per Airflow's own docs — meaning a pool sized for a fragile source (the previous topic) is not consumed by tasks that are merely deferred and waiting, only by tasks actually executing against that source. A reader carrying topic five's pool model forward might assume otherwise.

HITL and Deadline Alerts shipping in the same Airflow 3.1 release, both built on deferral, is not a coincidence of timing — it reflects the same underlying realization: 'pause and wait for something external, without burning a worker' is a general-purpose primitive, not a sensor-specific one, and both features are consumers of that primitive rather than reimplementations of it.

The hook's hundred-sensor scenario and the lab's twelve-task measurement are deliberately different scales for the same reason topic five's hook and lab differed: a hundred sensors establishes a scenario large enough to matter operationally, while twelve tasks is sized to let every defer/resume timestamp be read cleanly from real logs within the session's own time budget.

A reader might assume the ninety-five-percent worker-time reduction measured here is specific to a fifteen-second wait and would shrink for longer waits. The opposite is true: the fixed cost (a brief worker claim to start the defer, a brief one to resume) stays roughly constant regardless of wait length, so the percentage reduction only grows as the wait gets longer.

Trigger serialization encrypts sensitive kwargs since Airflow 2.9.0 (per the sourced docs), which is a separate concern from this topic's own finding: encryption protects a serializable secret from being read in plaintext in the database, but does nothing for an argument that isn't serializable in the first place — the two problems are easy to conflate but orthogonal.
